newsitem.title: USA: Seven letter bombs found in U.S., FBI issues alert.
newsitem.headline: Seven letter bombs found in U.S., FBI issues alert.

text.p: Seven letter bombs disguised as Christmas cards and mailed from the Middle East were found in three different locations in the United States on Thursday, prompting the FBI to warn Americans to be on alert.
"We are concerned that there could be additional such letters in the mail," FBI official Ray Mislock told a news conference.
Four letter bombs hidden inside Christmas cards and designed to detonate when opened were removed from the downtown Washington office of an Arab newspaper.

A fifth bomb addressed to the newspaper was intercepted after police and bomb technicians alerted the city's main post office in Northeast Washington, the central point for the city's mail distribution, Mislock said.
Two similar devices also were found at the federal prison in Leavenworth, Kansas, addressed to the parole officer.

The first of two letter bombs was discovered by an employee of the Saudi-owned newspaper Al-Hayat as he was opening the morning mail and noticed wires protruding from an envelope, police said. A second was found in that mail.
Another two arrived at the same 11th floor office in the afternoon postal delivery at the National Press building, two blocks from the White House.

The FBI Terrorist Task Force and the metropolitan police closed off a two-block area, evacuated the building which houses the Washington offices of many U.S. and foreign news organisations, and searched it with bomb sniffing dogs. Later on Thursday, it was reopened.
All four devices were put into special containers and taken away in reinforced bomb trucks belonging to the police department's Explosive Ordnance Division.
They were taken in a heavily escorted convoy to the parking lot of a football stadium and "disrupted" so the components could be studied for evidence, D.C. police spokesman Joe Gentile said.
"It is my understanding that they could have taken a life," he told reporters.
The FBI revealed later that two similar letter bombs also disguised as Christmas cards were found at Leavenworth prison.

Mislock and other FBI officials declined to confirm reports that they were investigating a possible connection between the cards and key figures in the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Centre and the foiled plot to bomb other New York landmarks.

Mohammad Salameh and Victor Alvarez were among 10 militant Moslems convicted in October 1995 of seditious conspiracy, bombing conspiracy and attempted bombing, and sentenced to life terms. Sources close to the case said Salameh and Alvarez were serving their terms in Leavenworth.
The FBI said none of the seven letter bombs found Thursday exploded but that they would have caused "grave harm" if detonated.

All of the cards were sent through the mail from Egypt. Some were postmarked Dec. 21, 1996, from Alexandria, Egypt and contained no return address. The FBI described them as plain white envelopes, 5 1/2 inches (14 cms) by 6 1/2 inches (16.5 cms) with computer generated addresses.
"Anyone receiving similar cards should use extreme caution, not handle the envelopes in any way and immediately notify the local police or local FBI office," the FBI statement said.
Law enforcement officials declined to describe the actual composition of the devices, but said "the components did make up a complete circuitry system for a bomb."
Al-Hayat, a Saudi newspaper based in London, had published the manifesto of a radical Islamic group after the fatal June 25 bombing of U.S. military personnel in the Saudi city of Khobar.
An Al-Hayat editor in London told CNN he had no idea who might have sent the letter bombs and said the newspaper supported moderate Arab regimes and opposed Islamic extremists.
